items.title: The Supersonic Fallacy
items.question: The sunk-cost fallacy is nicknamed the Concorde fallacy after the Anglo-French jetliner program continued despite mounting losses.
items.correctExplanation: True. Concorde flew on after economics failed: prestige plus spent billions overruled arithmetic. Nicknames commemorate famous traps.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The jet lost money nearly every year yet flew for decades: abandoning billions felt worse than losing millions yearly. History's costliest loyalty program.
items.lessonContent:
Prestige plus spent billions overrule arithmetic.
Loyalty programs cost history dearly.
Nicknames commemorate famous traps well.
Abandoning feels worse than bleeding.
Share this: name one flying Concorde.

items.title: The Sacrifice Ledger
items.question: During Vietnam, leaders invoked past American sacrifices as reasons to continue fighting rather than withdraw.
items.correctExplanation: True. Fallen soldiers became arguments against exit: McNamara and successors priced credibility in sunk lives. Ledgers of the dead funded further dying.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'Their sacrifice must not be in vain' converted losses into reasons for losses: escalation's moral arithmetic. Sacrifice-ledgers fund folly reliably.
items.lessonContent:
Fallen become arguments against exit.
Vain-avoidance funds further dying.
Moral arithmetic escalates reliably.
Ledgers of dead demand living interest.
Share this: audit one sacrifice ledger.

items.title: The Dollar Spiral
items.question: In Shubik's dollar auction — $1 auctioned to the highest bidder, runner-up also paying — final prices routinely exceed one dollar.
items.correctExplanation: True. Top two bidders both pay, so quitting wastes bids already placed: spirals past face value are standard. Auction design manufactures escalation.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Runner-up-pays converts auctions into traps: each bid protects prior bids, climbing past the prize. Classrooms pay $5 for $1 routinely.
items.lessonContent:
Top-two-pays manufactures spirals reliably.
Protecting bids climbs past prizes.
Design traps bidders structurally here.
Face values fall to sunk logic.
Share this: auction one dollar tonight.

items.title: The Responsibility Trap
items.question: Staw found that personal responsibility for an initial decision deepens commitment to failing courses — choosers escalate more than inheritors.
items.correctExplanation: True. Self-justification fuels escalation: admitting error costs more than funding failure. Choosers defend; inheritors cut.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Responsibility binds: decision-makers double down where successors walk away. Ego invests alongside capital, then outspends it.
items.lessonContent:
Ego invests alongside capital always.
Choosers defend; inheritors cut cleanly.
Admitting error costs more than funding.
Responsibility binds decisions tightly.
Share this: inherit one decision freshly.

items.title: The Good Money
items.question: 'Throwing good money after bad' describes investing further specifically to justify or rescue past spending.
items.correctExplanation: True. The idiom names escalation precisely: fresh funds drafted to vindicate sunk ones. Rescue missions for money already gone.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Good money follows bad hoping vindication: each round defends the last. Idioms encode economics folk-wisely.
items.lessonContent:
Fresh funds vindicate sunk ones vainly.
Rescue missions chase gone money.
Idioms encode economics folk-wisely.
Good follows bad downhill reliably.
Share this: halt one good-money march.

items.title: The Justified Hole
items.question: The need to justify past choices to oneself and others deepens commitment to failing courses of action.
items.correctExplanation: True. Self-justification converts errors into identities: abandoning means confessing. Holes deepen to protect diggers' pride.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Dissonance funds failing projects: quitting indicts the quitter. Pride digs where arithmetic would fill.
items.lessonContent:
Pride digs where arithmetic fills.
Quitting indicts quitters painfully.
Errors become identities needing defense.
Justification deepens holes steadily.
Share this: confess one sunk error.

items.title: The Imagined Funeral
items.question: Klein's premortem — imagining a project has already failed, then explaining why — reduces escalation by licensing doubt in advance.
items.correctExplanation: True. Prospective hindsight legitimizes dissent before commitment hardens: funerals imagined prevent real ones.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Premortems license what meetings punish: voicing failure modes early, when exits stay cheap. Doubt in advance beats regret after.
items.lessonContent:
Doubt in advance beats regret after.
Funerals imagined prevent real ones.
Dissent licensed early stays cheap.
Hindsight prospected prevents escalation.
Share this: hold one premortem today.

items.title: The Exit Contract
items.question: Preset kill criteria — exit rules written before investing — reliably curb escalation by deciding in calm weather.
items.correctExplanation: True. Ulysses contracts bind future selves: calm-weather rules override storm-weather rationalizing. Precommitment beats willpower.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Kill criteria decide exits before attachment forms: storms later cannot rewrite calm contracts. Decide cold to quit hot correctly.
items.lessonContent:
Calm contracts override storm rationalizing.
Precommitment beats willpower reliably.
Decide cold to quit hot correctly.
Exits preset survive attachment.
Share this: write one kill criterion.

items.title: The Blind Ledger
items.question: Escalating decision-makers systematically ignore opportunity costs — what else the committed money and years could accomplish.
items.correctExplanation: True. Escalation accounting omits roads not taken: visible losses debated, invisible alternatives ignored. Blind ledgers balance falsely.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Opportunity costs stay invisible while sunk costs glare: ledgers record spending, never forgone gains. Blindness to alternatives funds persistence.
items.lessonContent:
Invisible alternatives fund persistence.
Ledgers record spending, never forgone gains.
Opportunity blindness balances falsely.
Roads not taken need pricing too.
Share this: price one road not taken.

items.title: The Overrun Law
items.question: Megaprojects systematically overrun budgets while underdelivering benefits — Flyvbjerg's iron law of doomed big builds.
items.correctExplanation: True. Dams, rails, stadiums: over budget, over time, under benefits — systematically. Iron laws describe, then warn.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Flyvbjerg's databases prove the pattern across continents and decades: strategic misrepresentation plus optimism lock in losers. Bigness guarantees overruns statistically.
items.lessonContent:
Bigness guarantees overruns statistically.
Optimism locks in losers early.
Databases prove patterns anecdotes hide.
Iron laws describe, then warn.
Share this: discount one megaproject.

items.title: The Cancelled Collider
items.question: Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider in 1993 despite roughly $2 billion already spent on it.
items.correctExplanation: True. The SSC died with billions buried in Texas: a rare triumph of forward-looking over sunk reasoning. Holes stopped being dug.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Two billion sunk did not save the collider: Congress quit correctly, proving escape possible. Precedents of quitting deserve celebration.
items.lessonContent:
Quitting correctly deserves celebration.
Holes stop being dug sometimes.
Precedents prove escape possible.
Forward-looking beats sunk reasoning.
Share this: praise one great cancellation.

items.title: The Bygone Rule
items.question: Rational choice treats sunk costs as bygones — relevant to neither future costs nor future benefits.
items.correctExplanation: True. Bygones are bygones: only forward differences decide rationally. Past payments exit all equations.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Sunk costs appear on no future ledger: rational agents compare futures, never histories. Bygones rule all sound decisions.
items.lessonContent:
Pasts exit all future equations.
Futures compared, histories ignored.
Bygones rule sound decisions fully.
Forward differences decide alone.
Share this: bygone one sunk cost.

items.title: The Tactical Retreat
items.question: Grit means passion plus perseverance for ultimate goals — which permits abandoning tactics that fail, since goals outrank methods.
items.correctExplanation: True. Duckworth's grit aims at summits, not paths: quitting dead trails serves the mountain. Stubbornness about means betrays ends.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Grit perseveres in direction, flexes in method: tactical retreats advance strategic summits. Never-quit-anything misreads perseverance completely.
items.lessonContent:
Direction perseveres; methods flex freely.
Summits outrank trails always.
Tactical retreats advance strategy.
Stubborn means betray flexible ends.
Share this: retreat one tactic wisely.

items.title: The Pot Prison
items.question: Pot-committed poker players should always call any further bet, since folding wastes chips already committed.
items.correctExplanation: False. Committed chips are gone either way: calling needs pot odds, never history. Prisons are mental; exits stay open.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Pot-committed' confuses sunk chips with live odds: each call needs fresh justification. Folding freedoms survive all prior bets.
items.lessonContent:
Fresh calls need fresh justification.
Sunk chips never argue for calls.
Odds decide; histories watch silently.
Exits stay open despite priors.
Share this: fold one committed hand.

items.title: The Falling Knife
items.question: Averaging down on losing stocks — buying more as prices fall — always recovers the losses eventually.
items.correctExplanation: False. Falling knives cut catchers: losers often keep losing, and doubling down doubles exposure. Recovery is hoped, never owed.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Always' breaks on bankruptcies: averaging down concentrates risk in proven losers. Knives fall faster than catchers calculate.
items.lessonContent:
Losers often keep losing steadily.
Doubling down doubles exposure too.
Recovery hoped, never owed, arrives.
Knives cut optimistic catchers.
Share this: catch no falling knives.

items.title: The Tunnel Triumph
items.question: The Channel Tunnel beat its construction budgets and traffic forecasts comfortably, delighting investors.
items.correctExplanation: False. Costs roughly doubled while traffic disappointed for years: triumph arrived decades late, if at all. Boring succeeded; budgeting failed.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Overruns met underuse: investors waited a generation for returns. Tunnels bore through rock and forecasts alike.
items.lessonContent:
Boring succeeds; budgeting fails often.
Overruns meet underuse regularly.
Triumphs arrive decades late sometimes.
Forecasts tunnel vision reliably.
Share this: discount one tunnel vision.

items.title: The Cheap Opera
items.question: Sydney's Opera House finished quickly and under its original budget.
items.correctExplanation: False. Fourteen times over budget across fourteen years, architect exiled: icons cost what icons cost. Sails bill by decades.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Original estimates covered a fraction: Utzon left, costs multiplied, years accumulated. Cheap-and-fast belongs to other buildings.
items.lessonContent:
Icons cost what icons cost.
Estimates cover fractions routinely.
Sails bill by decades, not years.
Cheap-and-fast builds elsewhere.
Share this: budget one icon honestly.

items.title: The Profitable Games
items.question: Montreal profited quickly and handsomely from hosting the 1976 Olympics.
items.correctExplanation: False. The Big Owe: debt until 2006, thirty years of taxpayer installments. Profits arrived never; bills stayed.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Montreal's Olympics cost citizens three decades: 'profitable Games' ranks among history's optimistic phrases. Rings rust; debts compound.
items.lessonContent:
Rings rust while debts compound.
Optimistic phrases cost decades here.
Profits promised, installments delivered.
Games end; bills begin marathons.
Share this: audit one Olympic bid.

items.title: The Preserved Prize
items.question: All-pay contests — where every bidder pays win or lose — preserve the prize's full value for society overall.
items.correctExplanation: False. Aggregate bids dissipate the prize: rent-seeking burns value competing for transfers. Contests consume what prizes promise.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Tullock dissipation: total spending approaches prize value, vaporizing surplus. Everyone pays, one wins, society loses the difference.
items.lessonContent:
Spending approaches prizes wastefully.
Surplus vaporizes in contests fully.
Everyone pays; one wins; all lose.
Dissipation is rent-seeking's signature.
Share this: skip one all-pay contest.

items.title: The Unique Lab
items.question: Rival laboratories essentially never duplicate each other's research spending in patent races.
items.correctExplanation: False. Patent races duplicate massively: parallel labs burn parallel budgets chasing single prizes. Redundancy is the system's signature waste.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Winners take patents; losers' spending vanishes: races guarantee duplication. Parallel budgets chase singular prizes routinely.
items.lessonContent:
Parallel budgets chase singular prizes.
Redundancy signatures mark patent races.
Losers' spending vanishes entirely.
Duplication is systemic, not accidental.
Share this: share one research lead.

items.title: The Patient Loss
items.question: Cutting losses early is always the wrong move in investing — patience invariably rewards holders.
items.correctExplanation: False. 'Always' breaks both ways: patience rewards some holdings, rots others. Rules need conditions, never absolutes.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Invariably is invariably wrong: early exits save some portfolios, doom others. Absolutes mislead in both directions equally.
items.lessonContent:
Absolutes mislead both directions equally.
Invariably is invariably wrong here.
Conditions govern exits, never slogans.
Patience rewards some, rots others.
Share this: condition one exit rule.

items.title: The Golden Years
items.question: Years already invested can never keep anyone in a harmful relationship — people always leave promptly when harmed.
items.correctExplanation: False. Invested years anchor harmful bonds: 'after all this time' outvotes present pain. Sunk years chain as surely as sunk dollars.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Prompt leaving is the exception: shared histories, homes, and decades weigh exits down. Time invested binds like money spent.
items.lessonContent:
Shared histories weigh exits down.
Time invested binds like money.
Prompt leaving is the rare exception.
Years anchor harmful bonds sadly.
Share this: free one anchored heart.

items.title: The Honored Sunk
items.question: Fully rational decisions should count sunk costs alongside future costs when weighing options.
items.correctExplanation: False. Counting bygones corrupts every comparison: rational ledgers exclude the unrecoverable. Honor belongs to people, never to sunk dollars.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Sunk-inclusive math double-charges the past: options differ only ahead. Textbooks unanimous: bygones exit equations.
items.lessonContent:
Bygones exit all equations fully.
Double-charging pasts corrupts choices.
Honor people, never sunk dollars.
Unanimous textbooks agree here.
Share this: uncount one sunk dollar.

items.title: The Flying Profit
items.question: Concorde earned steady, handsome profits for its operators across its service life.
items.correctExplanation: False. Supersonic prestige bled money nearly throughout: speed sold tickets, economics never closed. Profits promised, losses delivered.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Concorde's books ran red across decades: fast, beloved, unprofitable. Prestige flies; arithmetic grounds.
items.lessonContent:
Prestige flies; arithmetic grounds always.
Speed sells tickets, never profits.
Beloved losers fill aviation history.
Fast, famous, unprofitable: the trio.
Share this: ground one prestige project.

items.title: The Money Trap
items.question: Escalation dynamics affect money only — time, lives, and reputations are immune to sunk-cost logic.
items.correctExplanation: False. Years, soldiers, and honor escalate exactly like dollars: sunk logic colonizes every currency. Immunity exists nowhere.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Wars, careers, and marriages escalate identically: unrecoverable investments bind all domains. Dollars merely illustrate universal dynamics.
items.lessonContent:
Unrecoverable binds all domains equally.
Dollars illustrate universal dynamics.
Immunity exists nowhere to sunk logic.
Currencies differ; traps repeat.
Share this: spot one non-money trap.
